target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for the workers most constrained by work.
objection: A federal holiday does not by itself guarantee paid time off or workplace closure for private employees, especially in retail, food service, and other hourly jobs, so low-income workers may still have to work or lose pay and therefore may not benefit in practice.

target: AG1’s assumption that making Election Day a holiday is the most practical way to increase participation.
objection: More direct policies, such as laws requiring employers to provide time off to vote with pay protections and automatic/opt-out voter registration, are more reliable ways to raise turnout than a holiday alone.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce schedule conflict because schools and workplaces would be less likely to operate normally.
objection: That underestimates the fact that low-income hourly workers are concentrated in essential or open-on-holidays jobs, so a holiday would not reliably free the people most likely to face voting barriers.

target: AG1’s idea that a national holiday would lower the practical costs of voting for hourly workers.
objection: Calling Election Day a holiday changes the calendar but not wages or schedules for private-sector workers, so they may still have to choose between voting time and earnings or paid time off.

target: AG1’s proposal to combine holiday status with paid voting protections as part of the same approach.
objection: If paid time and voting protections are added, then those worker protections—not the holiday—are doing the real work; the holiday becomes redundant and may distract from the more direct policy.

target: AG1’s argument that the holiday would also solve school, childcare, and caregiving scheduling barriers.
objection: Even with a holiday, low-income parents may still face childcare, transportation, and service-schedule problems, and private employers can keep workers on duty, so the household-schedule benefit is incomplete.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status lowers “transaction costs” by reducing the need for employees to request time off.
objection: Transaction costs are not eliminated unless private employers are required to close or pay workers; otherwise employees still must request time, face possible denial, and navigate pay tradeoffs.

target: AG1’s framing of the policy as complementary rather than redundant when paired with worker protections.
objection: If the package includes enforceable paid time-to-vote protections, the holiday is mostly redundant and can create legislative risk that weakens the more important enforcement provisions.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday will meaningfully improve access through changed defaults and reduced uncertainty.
objection: Holiday status does not actually give private-sector workers guaranteed paid time off, so hourly employees can still face the same uncertainty, pay loss, and employer discretion that suppress turnout.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday changes the labor-market environment and makes employers more likely to grant paid time or reduce hours in ways that help voters.
objection: Holiday status only changes the date label; it does not ensure pay continuity, and employers may simply keep shifts running or reduce hours, leaving low-income workers with the same voting-versus-pay tradeoff.

target: AG1’s additional claim that a holiday would ease election administration and reduce waits by making more people available on Election Day.
objection: Even if more people are off work, a national holiday still does not reliably address the unequal work/pay barrier facing low-income workers, so administrative convenience does not solve the core inequity.
